"Asif, you were wheezing at the match. Where was your inhaler?"
"In my bag. In the car park."
"Why?"
"Because if I use it in front of the team they'll treat me like I'm made of glass."
Gopika, his friend from the mixed team, pulled her knees up and sat down beside him on the bench. "I get it. You want to be just another player."
"Yes! Not the sick kid."
"Okay. Then what would make it easier? Not your mum's rules. Yours."
Asif thought. "If it's in my kit bag by the bench, I can use it during water break. Nobody really looks then."
"That works. And if it gets worse, you stop and use it anyway. If the wheezing keeps coming back, you tell your doctor. Deal?"
"Deal."
"Should I tell Coach?"
"No. I'll tell him myself."
"Fair. That's your call."

qa.a: It was in his bag, in the car park.

qa.q: Why did Asif keep his inhaler away from the team?
qa.a: He was worried they would treat him like he was made of glass, and he wanted to feel like just another player.

qa.q: Why did Gopika's approach work better than a set of rules?
qa.a: She understood his wish for dignity, let him design the plan, and only added that he must use it if things get worse.

qa.q: How does Gopika see Asif's wish to be just another player?
qa.a: She understands and respects it, while still caring about his safety, so she lets him decide who to tell.

passage:
On the school trip to Ooty last winter, I skipped my evening medicine two days running. Everyone was in the hostel room laughing, and I didn't want to be the one who had to go off and take pills. I told myself I felt fine.
By the third day I felt awful: shaky, tired, cranky. Ammi kept texting, "Did you take it, beta?" every few hours, which made me want to hide more.
My friend Rehana noticed I was quiet on the bus. She didn't lecture. She just asked, "Do you want me to come with you when you take it, so it's normal?" After that I told the teacher too, and she found me a quiet corner.
When I got home, Ammi and I agreed on one check-in text a day, and I'd manage the rest myself. It felt like being trusted.

Tanvir

qa.q: How many days running did Tanvir skip the medicine?
qa.a: Tanvir skipped the evening medicine two days running.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir skip the medicine on the trip?
qa.a: Tanvir felt embarrassed and did not want to stand out in front of the others in the hostel room.

qa.q: What was the turning point that helped Tanvir manage the condition?
qa.a: Rehana's offer to come along made taking medicine feel normal, and telling the teacher brought a quiet space; later, trust from Ammi gave Tanvir some independence.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt during the trip?
qa.a: She was probably worried, which is why she kept texting, but her frequent messages made Tanvir want to hide.

grounding: It shows a teenager with a long-term condition skipping treatment to avoid standing out, and how respectful support from a friend and more trust at home help.

passage: Tuan, fifteen, had asthma, but nobody on his Oslo football team knew. He hid his inhaler in his jacket and skipped it before matches, because he hated the thought of anyone seeing. During a hard game in the cold, his chest went tight and he had to stop, bent over and wheezing. His coach, Ulla, jogged over. She didn't make a fuss. 'Where's your inhaler?' He pointed. She brought the jacket, then stood so the others couldn't see. Afterwards she sat with him. 'You don't have to tell the team anything. But I need you safe. What would make it easier for you?' Tuan thought. 'If I could use it in the changing room before, without questions.' 'Deal. Your choice who knows.' He nodded, relieved.

qa.a: In his jacket.

qa.q: Why did Tuan skip his inhaler before matches?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and afraid of standing out if anyone saw him use it.

qa.q: What made Ulla's approach work?
qa.a: She respected Tuan's privacy, asked what would make it easier and let him choose, while making his safety clear.

qa.q: How might Tuan's teammates have reacted if Ulla had announced his asthma?
qa.a: They might have stared or treated him differently, which is exactly what Tuan feared.

passage: In the school nurse's room, Preeti, sixteen, sat with her arms crossed. She had type 1 diabetes and had stopped doing her lunchtime blood checks because her friends stared when she used the kit in the canteen. That morning she'd felt shaky in chemistry. Devika Ma'am, the nurse, didn't lecture. 'You're sixteen. You know your body better than I do. What's getting in the way?' Preeti stared at the floor. 'Everyone watches. I just want to be normal.' Devika nodded. 'That makes sense. What if you did your checks here, in private, whenever you like? No one needs to know unless you tell them.' Preeti looked up. 'Really?' 'Your plan, your choice. I'm just here if you need me.' The next day Preeti came in at lunch, on her own.

passage:
Dear Coach Francis,
I'm writing because I can't say this properly at practice. Since you found out about my condition, you've benched me every time I look tired, and you ask me in front of everyone if I've taken my tablets. I know you mean well. But it makes me feel like a patient, not a player. Last month I even stopped mentioning when I felt dizzy, because I didn't want to be benched. That was stupid, I know.
Here's what I'd like instead. I take my tablets every morning. If I feel unwell, I'll tell you quietly and sit out. You don't need to ask in front of the team. My doctor says I can play.
Can we try it for a month?
Tushar

qa.q: When does Tushar take the tablets?
qa.a: Every morning.

qa.q: How does Tushar feel when asked about tablets in front of everyone?
qa.a: Tushar feels embarrassed and treated like a patient, not a player.

qa.q: What plan does Tushar propose?
qa.a: Tushar will take the tablets every morning and quietly tell the coach and sit out when unwell, without public questions.

qa.q: How might Coach Francis feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Coach Francis may feel surprised and a little hurt, but also relieved that Tushar wants to be honest about feeling unwell.

grounding: Shows a teenager who hid symptoms to avoid being singled out, asking for support that respects independence and dignity rather than control.

passage: Bhupen, you asked why I used to vanish before PE. Okay. I'm Gurleen, I've had asthma since I was little, and in Class 9 I decided I was done being "the inhaler kid". I left it in my locker. When my chest got tight during the relay, I pretended I had a stitch and sat out, wheezing quietly behind the water tank. One day it got bad and Coach Sandhu found me. I expected a scene. Instead she sat down, waited till I could breathe, and asked, "What would make carrying it easier for you?" We worked it out together: a small pouch on my belt, my choice when to step out, no announcements. That same afternoon I told the school nurse too. Now I run the relay. Some days I still hate it. But it's mine to manage.

qa.a: Behind the water tank.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen leave the inhaler in the locker?
qa.a: Gurleen felt embarrassed and tired of being "the inhaler kid", and wanted to be treated as normal.

qa.q: What made Coach Sandhu's response work?
qa.a: She asked what would help instead of taking control, and they planned a belt pouch and private choices together, respecting Gurleen's dignity.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Gurleen after hearing this story?
qa.a: Bhupen would probably understand the vanishing before PE and respect Gurleen for managing it with dignity.
